\chapter{Tenia and Tuve --- When the Tense Changes the Meaning}
\label{ch:aspect-changes-meaning}
\hlchaptermodality{99}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say why tuve una casa means I got one, and predict what a state verb's preterite will mean.}

Complete ES-C48-tenia-tuve: contrast tenia and tuve, and say what any state verb's preterite will mean.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tenía / tuve]{tenía and tuve — when the tense changes the meaning}

\label{lesson:ES-C48-tenia-tuve}



\begin{quote}
So far the two pasts have shown you the same event from two places. With one very common verb, they show you two \textbf{different} events.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: having, and getting}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Tenía} una casa.} — I \textbf{had} a house. \emph{\textbf{Tuve} una casa.} — I \textbf{got} a house.
\end{quote}

Read those twice. The second one is not \textquotedblleft{}I had a house, viewed as finished.\textquotedblright{} It is a different verb in English altogether.

The reason follows from everything you already know. \emph{Tener} means a \textbf{state} — having something is not an event, it is a condition that simply continues. So the imperfect, which has no edges, fits it perfectly: \emph{tenía} is the ordinary way to say you had something.

Force that state into the preterite and you are demanding edges for something that does not have any. Spanish resolves the clash the only way it can: \textbf{it gives you the moment the state began.} The edge of \emph{having} is \emph{getting}.

Nothing irregular is happening. It is the same aspect rule you met two chapters ago, applied to a verb where the result is a new word in English.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
This is worth more than one verb, because the same thing happens to every verb that names a state rather than an action. When you meet those verbs later, you will not need a list — you will already know what their preterite is going to mean: \textbf{the moment the state started.}

It also explains a frustration you may already have had. English \textquotedblleft{}I had\textquotedblright{} covers both sentences above, so an English speaker reaching for \emph{tuve} is often reaching for the wrong one. The fix is not to memorise which is which. It is to notice that you are describing a \textbf{state}, and states live in the imperfect unless you specifically mean the moment they began.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tenía una casa\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Tuve una casa\textquotedblright{} — hear the English change
  \item the rule aloud — a state in the preterite gives you its beginning
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Tenía una casa}? (I \textbf{had} one.) \emph{Tuve una casa}? (I \textbf{got} one.) And why? (A state forced into the preterite gives you the \textbf{moment it began}.) Next: all of it in one place.
\end{tcolorbox}
